correctness.rationale: For a PSD contraction P, P²≤P gives squared off-diagonal row mass ≤q(1−q) with q=Pii. Cauchy–Schwarz and writing q=(1+x)/2 show the exact row-sum bound (1+sqrt(n))/2: x+sqrt(n−1)sqrt(1−x²) has maximum sqrt(n). The positive rank-one projection attains it in row one, with q=(1+1/sqrt(n))/2, and the n=1 case agrees directly. Normalize each nonzero power A^j by b^j to use the same lemma. The derivative expansion has two one-sided terms and k−2 two-sided terms with the announced row/column bounds. At bP, using the all-ones symmetric perturbation J, row-one products attain every term with the same sign since P^j=P; the first-order term also attains its bound. Move the base point strictly inside by (b−epsilon)P+epsilon(I−P) before taking the directional limit, so the upper/lower spectral caps hold for admissible distinct test pairs. Norm convergence of the series and its derivative follows from radius >b and allows integration on the convex segment. Geometric sums give the stated resolvent square, and constants/affine series and n=1 specialize correctly.
residual_risks: Sharpness is a supremum, not necessarily equality for separated inputs; proof uses real symmetry, two spectral caps and nonnegative Taylor coefficients. The sampled b-scaled resolvent test is only corroboration, not a sharpness proof for that mapping.

Sharpness for one common direction over an entire class separates the exact coefficient from loose norm conversions; the resolvent shows a strict effect of the lower spectral cap compared with the known half-line expression.
